brief: A kitchen herb planter: two or three bins on a base, filled with soil and planted with basil and thyme.

requirements.evidence: Three full base pieces in a triangle at (0,0), (1,0) and (0,1), level 0. The three shared walls are joined with joint bolts (jointBolt:0#0,0#0, 0#0,0#5, 0#1,0#4), which cleared the loose-body warnings.

requirements.requirement: Two or three bins on the base
requirements.evidence: Three full-depth drained bins (hex-bin-full-drain), one in each base cell.
fillSoil was applied to all three bins.

Basil (basil-harvest) is in bin 0,0,0. Thyme is in bin 1,0,0 (thyme-harvest) and bin 0,1,0 (thyme-young). I tried a second plant beside the basil in bin 0,1,0, but it was refused because the plants overlapped, so each bin has one plant.

requirements.requirement: Suitable for kitchen use (indoor planter, food herbs)
requirements.evidence: The drained bins help with watering by their shape. The configurator only checks fit, so it can't confirm the printed material is food-safe, holds up to water or is waterproof. There is no drip tray, so water from the drain holes may reach the counter.

finish.summary: I built a three-bin herb planter: three base pieces in a triangle, bolted together, with a drained full-depth bin in each. All three bins are filled with soil. One has basil and two have thyme. The build check passed with no rule errors and no mesh collisions.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
